# njord

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

**njord** is an R package for parametric windstorm trigger design and basis
risk quantification, focusing on the UK market. It provides a reproducible
pipeline from reanalysis hazard data through to the design and evaluation of
index-based insurance triggers with explicit modelling of the gap between
parametric payouts and indemnity losses.

## Background

Parametric (index-based) insurance pays out when a measurable physical index
exceeds a contractual threshold rather than when a policyholder files a
claim. For natural catastrophes such as European windstorms, this removes
loss-adjustment delays and moral hazard but introduces *basis risk*: the
payout may not match the insured's actual loss either because the storm was
severe locally but the index was low or vice versa. Quantifying and
decomposing that gap is the central challenge in parametric product design.

This package implements a reference workflow for a UK windstorm parametric
trigger:

1. **Hazard** — reanalysis-derived wind gust footprints for all named storms 
   since 1940, giving the maximum 3-second 10-metre gust (m s⁻¹) at each grid 
   cell over a 72-hour window centred on the storm’s peak land impact.
2. **Exposure and vulnerability** — gridded asset exposure (LitPop) combined
   with the Schwierz et al. (2010) damage model to estimate indemnity losses
   for each storm event.
3. **Trigger** — a UK-wide area-weighted mean peak gust index with a linear
   ramp payout between an attachment and exhaustion level.
4. **Basis risk** — the distribution of the difference between parametric
   payout and modelled indemnity loss across the historical event set and
   its decomposition by source.

## Data

### ERA5 windstorm reanalysis

Hazard data come from the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) Enhanced
Windstorm Service (EWS) dataset
(`sis-european-wind-storm-reanalysis`; van den Brink, 2019;
Copernicus Climate Change Service, 2025), derived from the ERA5 global
reanalysis (Hersbach et al., 2020).

For each identified storm event the dataset provides:

- **Footprints** — the maximum 3-second 10-metre wind gust (m s⁻¹) over a
  72-hour window centred on the storm's peak land impact, 
  on a 0.25° × 0.25° grid (~28 km). Njord uses the native ERA5 
  resolution (0.25°) product. Each footprint is restricted to a 
  1000 km radius around the storm track to avoid 
  cross-contamination between contemporaneous events.

- **Track catalogue** — 6-hourly positions, mean sea level pressure and
  10 m gust speed at the storm centre for all tracked systems 1940–2025.
  Two tracking algorithms are available: *Hodges* (TRACK; Hodges, 1995, 1999)
  which follows 850 hPa relative vorticity and *TempestExtremes*
  which tracks MSLP minima. Njord uses the Hodges product, consistent with
  CLIMADA's default configuration and Mishra et al. (2026).

- **Summary indicators** — pre-computed annual storm counts, mean gust,
  Storm Severity Index (SSI), normalised SSI, area ratio and wind gust
  ratio, aggregated by NUTS region (NUTS0/1/2) and wind speed threshold
  (0, 15.6, 20, 25 m s⁻¹) for 1940–2025 (~170 000 rows).

The footprint archive (downloaded via the `ecmwfr` package) currently
comprises **723 monthly zip files** (from footprints_hodges_194002.zip through to
footprints_hodges_202604.zip) each containing one or more NetCDF footprint
files for storms active in that calendar month.

## Vulnerability model

The **Schwierz et al. (2010)** damage model is used to estimate the mean
damage ratio (MDR) as a function of wind gust speed $v$:

$$\text{MDR}(v) = \text{MDD}(v) \times \text{PAA}(v)$$

where MDD (mean damage degree) is the expected fraction of asset value
destroyed given that the asset is affected and PAA (percentage of assets
affected) is the probability that an asset at this location suffers any
damage at all. Both are empirically derived nonlinear lookup tables,
originally calibrated against UK insurance losses from named storms in the
period 1987–1990 (Schwierz et al., 2010) and subsequently validated across
multiple European countries.

The model is implemented in the open-source
[CLIMADA](https://climada-python.readthedocs.io/) platform (ETH Zurich;
Aznar-Siguan and Bresch, 2019) as `ImpfStormEurope.from_schwierz()`; njord
uses the same curve nodes (`schwierz_mdr()`).

The MDR surface is multiplied pointwise with the LitPop asset exposure
(Eberenz et al., 2020) — a globally consistent 30 arcsec (~1 km) dataset
that disaggregates national asset values in proportion to nightlight intensity
× population — to yield modelled monetary losses per grid cell and per event.
The sum across the UK grid is the event-level **indemnity loss benchmark**.

### UK recalibration

Mishra et al. (2026) recalibrate the Schwierz model against PERILS industry
loss data (1999–2024) for 12 European countries using CLIMADA, with the same
hazard (C3S EWS footprints) and exposure (LitPop) as njord. One parameter is
fitted per country: the MDD curve is multiplied by a common factor and the
PAA is left unchanged. The fit is made separately with RMSE and RMSLE cost
functions. RMSE is driven by the largest events and fits the tail; RMSLE fits
the frequent, mid-range events. For the UK both lower the curve: the maximum
MDD is about 0.030 (RMSE) and 0.033 (RMSLE), against 0.0373 for the original,
factors of about 0.8 and 0.88. The paper gives these only in a figure
(Fig. 3m–n), so the factors are read by eye. njord uses `mdd_scale = 0.8`,
the RMSE fit, since the trigger is concerned with the tail.

## Reference trigger: UK-wide index

The reference parametric trigger in njord is a single **UK-wide
area-weighted mean peak gust index**, computed for each storm event as:

$$I = \frac{\sum_{i} w_i \cdot v_i}{\sum_i w_i}$$

where $v_i$ is the maximum 3-second gust at grid cell $i$ within the UK
boundary and $w_i$ is the cell area weight. This is conceptually equivalent
to the mean wind gust field in the C3S summary indicators but computed
directly from the footprint rasters rather than from the
pre-aggregated product.

The parametric payout follows a **linear ramp** structure:

$$P(I) = \begin{cases}
0 & I < A \\
L \cdot \dfrac{I - A}{E - A} & A \le I \le E \\
L & I > E
\end{cases}$$

where $A$ is the attachment (trigger) level, $E$ is the exhaustion level and
$L$ is the policy limit. The attachment and exhaustion are designed to be
calibrated against the historical loss distribution so that the trigger fires
at approximately the 1-in-5-year loss return period and reaches the limit at
approximately the 1-in-20-year level; these are illustrative targets that would
be negotiated in a real transaction.

## Basis risk

For each storm event $e$, the basis risk is defined as:

$$B_e = P_e - L_e$$

where $P_e$ is the parametric payout and $L_e$ is the modelled indemnity
loss, both expressed as a fraction of total insured value. Positive values
indicate over-payment (the insurer pays more than the loss); negative values
indicate under-payment (the insured bears a residual loss).

The distribution of $B_e$ across the historical event set characterises the
basis risk profile of the trigger design. Key summary statistics are the
mean (expected value of the basis risk, which should be close to zero for a
fair product) and the standard deviation and tail quantiles (which measure
the variability of the mismatch).

## Planned refinements

The reference UK-wide trigger is deliberately simple.
A number of refinements could be considered.

### 1. Zonal trigger (NUTS1 regions)

Rather than a single UK-wide index, compute a separate sub-index for each of
the 12 UK NUTS1 regions (e.g. Scotland, North West England, Wales, South East
England). The trigger fires if any one regional index exceeds its attachment.
This reduces geographic basis risk — the risk that a storm devastates one
region while the UK-wide average remains below the trigger threshold — at the
cost of additional complexity in the contract specification.

### 2. Multi-zone aggregate trigger

Extend the zonal approach to an aggregate structure: the payout is triggered
by a weighted sum of regional indices, with weights reflecting the insured
exposure distribution. This is analogous to the zonal SSI structures used in
some European cat bond transactions.

### 3. Trigger shape optimisation

The linear ramp is a natural starting point but not necessarily optimal. A
step trigger (binary payout at attachment) has maximum simplicity; a
polynomial ramp can be calibrated to match the indemnity loss curve more
closely in the tail. The optimal shape can be found by minimising the basis
risk variance subject to an actuarial fairness constraint using the
historical event set as training data.

### 4. Basis risk decomposition

Following Bouchard and Romanic (2023), the total basis risk variance can be
decomposed into:

- **Geographic basis risk** — mismatch between the location of losses and the
  spatial footprint measured by the trigger index.
- **Temporal basis risk** — mismatch arising from the 72-hour integration
  window versus the actual loss accumulation period.
- **Structural basis risk** — residual mismatch after controlling for
  geography and timing, attributable to differences in vulnerability (e.g.
  industrial vs residential exposure) not captured by the damage model.

### 5. Vulnerability sensitivity

Compare the basis risk under `mdd_scale` 1 (original), 0.8 (RMSE) and 0.88
(RMSLE). A single MDD factor scales every storm's loss alike, so the
attachment and exhaustion from `calibrate_trigger()` do not change; only the
size of losses against payouts does.

### 6. SSI-based trigger

Rather than a mean gust index, the trigger could be based on the Storm
Severity Index (Leckebusch et al., 2008):

$$\text{SSI} = \sum_i \left(\frac{v_i}{V98_i} - 1\right)^3 w_i$$

where the sum is over grid cells where $v_i > V98_i$ and $V98_i$ is the
98th percentile of the local gust distribution over a reference
climatological period (1991–2020). The SSI is more sensitive to extreme
local gusts than the area-weighted mean and better reflects the nonlinear
nature of wind damage. Computing it requires a V98 surface derived from
the footprint ensemble, which is preparatory work not yet complete.

### 7. Frequency–severity model and EP curves

A complete probabilistic view of the trigger requires modelling storm frequency
and severity separately. Storm frequency (annual event count above a minimum
gust threshold) would be fitted with a negative binomial distribution to
accommodate over-dispersion relative to a Poisson process. Storm severity
(modelled loss conditional on occurrence) would be fitted with a Generalised
Pareto Distribution to the exceedances above a threshold chosen by mean excess
plot inspection. Together these permit Monte Carlo simulation of an extended
event set from which occurrence and aggregate exceedance probability curves can
be derived for both indemnity losses and parametric payouts.

## Development environment

The package uses a [Nix flake](https://nixos.org/) to pin all system
dependencies (R, system libraries, fonts) to a reproducible state.
With Nix installed, enter the development shell with:

```bash
nix develop
```

ERA5 data are downloaded via the ECMWF Climate Data Store (CDS) API using
the [`ecmwfr`](https://bluegreen-labs.github.io/ecmwfr/) package. A CDS
account and personal access token are required:

```r
options(keyring_backend = "file")
ecmwfr::wf_set_key(user = "<your-cds-uid>", key = "<your-api-key>",
                   service = "cds")
```
